rv.q: This latest remount feels strangely hunkered down in itself, even as geysers of absurdity erupt willy-nilly.
Although Guare’s play remains quite funny, Cromer downplays most of its humor to ill effect.
So go for Kanin’s savvy script and for one truly inspired comic performance.
The tone is wrong -- distancing, unpleasant, not funny enough.

As played with anger and seething resentment by Stiller, Artie’s raspy cabaret act (delivered, in part, with Stiller’s back to the audience) is about as much fun as happy hour in the Holiday Inn in Hades.
Shockingly, Stiller conveys none of them, leaving a hole at the center of this unbalanced House of Blue Leaves.
Cromer leans too far toward the latter and misses the laughs.
This is one of the great American plays, and this production — the cast and direction — is worthy of its brilliance.
Ben Stiller has given Artie a new sense of desperation, Edie Falco has toned Bananas down to a human level, and Jennifer Jason Leigh brings new laughs to Bunny’s weird world.
But this overly muted rendition, while occasionally displaying moments of stunning theatricality, provides little of the sugar that would help its medicine go down.

Newcomers to “The House of Blue Leaves” are unlikely to see beyond Cromer’s misguided staging to appreciate the play itself while people who know and love it are advised to skip this unworthy occasion.

cn.t: Critics are divided on Cromer's somber revival of Guare's dark comedy, with praise for Falco's performance but concerns about tonal imbalance and clashing acting styles among the star-studded cast.

vs.sum: The Walter Kerr Theatre offers excellent sightlines and sound quality, making it a great venue for intimate productions. However, the comfort level is below average due to limited legroom and seat width, though the theater's Italian Renaissance-inspired decor adds to its charm.

acc.note: No elevators. All accessible seating on Orchestra level. Infrared headsets and audio induction neck loops.
